To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a novel method to systematically study cell signaling and that we have discovered major differences in signaling between normal and transformed human hepatocytes.
we developed a novel method to study the differences between primary and tumor cells, and that we used this method to study the inflammatory response of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells.

1) we developed a new experimental approach for studying the response of human primary cells to perturbations; 2) we used this approach to study the response of human hepatocytes and hepatoma cells to perturbants that induce inflammatory and proliferative responses; and 3) we found profound differences in the response of hepatocytes versus hepatoma cells to these perturbants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of systems biology approaches to the study of cell signaling.
the development of a new approach to network analysis and with the discovery of new insights into the molecular biology of hepatocellular carcinoma.
the analysis of cell signaling networks, with a focus on the immune system, and with a view toward the development of novel therapies for cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the differences in signaling between normal and transformed hepatocytes are profound, but that the specific details of these differences are complex and require further investigation.
the differences in network structure are consistent with the differences in cellular function, which is the ultimate goal of the study.
our data suggest a model of hepatocellular carcinoma in which the cancer cells have evolved to avoid immune detection by dampening the normal inflammatory and immune response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it provides a proof of principle that a systematic approach to biochemical network inference can be used to reveal differences in cell behavior.
we have used a combination of high throughput biochemical and computational methods to infer differences in signaling network topology between normal and transformed hepatocytes.
the network topology of signaling pathways differs between normal and transformed cells, and this difference is reflected by the cell's response to environmental stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of high throughput proteomics and cell signaling assays can be used to identify and characterize differences in signaling networks between normal and cancer cells.
the combination of systematic, high throughput, multiplexed biochemical analysis and comparative network modeling is a powerful way to understand differences in cellular signaling networks.
cell signaling networks can be inferred from a limited set of cell responses to environment and small molecule drugs.
